title: The impact of classroom design on pupils' learning: Final results of a holistic, multi-level analysis
research_question: To explore if there is any evidence for demonstrable impacts of school building design on the learning rates of pupils in primary schools.

participants.description: 3766 primary school pupils (Years 1-6) from 153 classrooms in 27 state-funded, mixed-gender schools across three diverse local authority areas (Blackpool, Hampshire, Ealing) in England, UK. Pupils' ages ranged from 5 to 11 years old. Sample included pupils with Free School Meals (FSM), English as an Additional Language (EAL), and Special Educational Needs (SEN).
participants.recruitment: Schools were chosen to have a wide spectrum of different architectures, built at different times and of different sizes, from three local authority areas in the UK.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 153 existing primary school classrooms (Years 1-6) in 27 schools. Classrooms varied in dimensions, window size/placement, door placement, Interactive Whiteboard (IWB), desk arrangement, learning zone layouts, control over environment (thermostat, AC), use of space, coat pegs, quality of desks/chairs, decorations/colors, visual complexity of displays. Whole school surveys also covered shared spaces (libraries, assembly halls, gyms, outdoor areas).

5-point rating scale based on classroom floor area/shape, breakout/storage space, learning zones, wall area for display

findings.mechanism: Higher starting scores correlate with less progress, reflecting non-linear learning rates over school life.

findings.antecedent: Weighted start-on-age (pupil's academic starting grade relative to age group)
findings.mechanism: Pupils with higher starting grades relative to their age group tend to make less progress.
Children in older classes made less progress, suggesting age-related differences in learning rates.

findings.antecedent: Months age (pupil's age relative to birthday in academic year)

findings.mechanism: Males and females did not make significantly different overall progress.
Socioeconomic disadvantage (FSM status) is associated with poorer academic progress.

findings.antecedent: EAL (English as an Additional Language) status
findings.mechanism: EAL pupils on average show significantly better overall progress, possibly due to rapid language acquisition in a new environment.
Pupils with SEN show poorer academic progress.
Natural light regulates sleep/wake cycles and optimum daylighting affects performance.
Noise levels in classrooms often exceed optimal for speech understanding, affecting attention.
Performance increased when temperature was reduced slightly.
Mental attention is slower with high CO2 levels, and performance is affected by low air exchange rates.
Experience of nature provides profound benefits for children, increasing mental plasticity.
Intimate and personalized spaces are better for absorbing information and foster feelings of responsibility.
Flexibility is needed to allow for different activities within the classroom and to address the needs of different users.
Clearly marked pathways to activity areas improve utilization of space and performance metrics.
Focused attention is crucial for learning; visual features in the classroom can tax still-developing and fragile ability to maintain task goals and ignore distractions.
Room colour has an effect on both emotions and physiology, causing mood swings that can impact performance.
Pupils in higher year groups made less progress, indicating non-linear learning rates.

findings.antecedent: Weighted Start-on-age (pupil's academic starting grade relative to age group)
findings.mechanism: Pupils who were advanced for their age group made more progress on average.

findings.antecedent: EAL (English as an Additional Language) status
findings.mechanism: EAL pupils performed significantly better in the multi-level model.
Children on FSM performed significantly worse in the multi-level model.
SEN pupils showed a significantly greater deficit in overall progress.
Optimum glazing size (considering orientation/glare) and high quality/quantity of electrical lighting improve visual environment and learning.
Rooms with little sun heat, adequate external shading, and central heating with thermostat control allow better thermal comfort and learning.
Greater room volume, more opening choices/bigger opening area, and mechanical ventilation improve air quality and learning.
Distinct design features, personalized displays, and ergonomic/good quality furniture foster a sense of ownership, supporting learning.
Varied plan shapes (age-appropriate), breakout/storage space, and well-defined learning zones support different learning methods and activities.
Overall visual diversity (layout, ceiling, displays) should be balanced, not too high or too sterile, showing a curvilinear effect for optimal learning.
Light/white walls with bright highlights/feature wall, and bright colours on furniture/displays as accents create good stimulation for learning.
Acoustics, despite bivariate correlation, were competed out in the multi-level model, suggesting its impact is integrated within other factors or less direct.
findings.quote: acoustics... were competed out in the MLM and so the evidence for their importance... can only be said to be weak.

findings.mechanism: Links to nature, despite bivariate correlation, were competed out in the multi-level model, suggesting its impact is integrated within other factors or less direct.
findings.quote: links to nature... were competed out in the MLM and so the evidence for their importance... can only be said to be weak.

findings.antecedent: Classroom environmental factors (Light, Temperature, Air Quality, Ownership, Flexibility, Complexity, Colour)
findings.mechanism: The combined effect of seven key design parameters from Naturalness, Individualisation, and Stimulation principles explains 16% of the total range of variability in pupils' academic progress.
findings.quote: The impact of the modelled classroom parameters was 16% of the total range of the variability in pupils' learning progress.

findings.antecedent: Naturalness design principle (Light, Temperature, Air Quality)
findings.consequent: Proportion of explained effect on Overall Progress model
findings.mechanism: Basic human comfort needs related to naturalness (light, thermal, air quality) are the most influential, accounting for 49% of the environmental impact.

findings.consequent: Proportion of explained effect on Overall Progress model
findings.mechanism: How well the classroom meets individual pupil needs and preferences accounts for 28% of the environmental impact.

findings.antecedent: Level of Stimulation design principle (Complexity, Colour)
findings.consequent: Proportion of explained effect on Overall Progress model
findings.mechanism: The appropriate level of visual excitement and vibrancy for learning activities accounts for 23% of the environmental impact.

findings.antecedent: School level factors (e.g., architecture, pupil intake)
findings.mechanism: Only 3% of the variance was at the school level, suggesting that pupil and classroom level factors dominate, supporting 'inside-out design'.
findings.quote: In the three level model only 3% of the variance was at the school level.

findings.antecedent: Full two-level MLM (pupil and classroom factors)
findings.mechanism: The combined pupil and classroom factors explain 58% of the variance in academic progress, indicating a good model fit.
findings.quote: The overall R-squared fit for the two-level model is 58%.

findings.antecedent: Classroom parameters (Light, Temperature, Air Quality, Ownership, Flexibility, Complexity, Colour)
findings.consequent: Overall Progress (range between most and least effective classrooms)
findings.mechanism: The difference in academic progress between the most and least effective classroom designs, holding pupil factors constant, is 7.93 NC points.
findings.quote: This gives a range of 7.93 in NC points for the variation in Overall Progress, solely driven by the physical features of the classroom environment.

mechanisms: The effect of the built environment on users is experienced via multiple sensory inputs, which are resolved in the users' brains, providing a basis for understanding combined effects.

The Naturalness principle relates to environmental parameters required for physical comfort (light, sound, temperature, air quality, links to nature) which directly impact physiological and cognitive functions.

The Individualisation principle relates to how well the classroom meets the needs of a particular group of children, fostering ownership, flexibility, and connection, which supports learning processes and behavior.
The Stimulation principle relates to how exciting and vibrant the classroom is, with appropriate levels of complexity and colour to maintain focused attention and avoid distraction.
Pupils' academic progress is dependent on a full range of factors drawn from across all three design principles (Naturalness, Individualisation, Stimulation).
The muted impact of the whole-building level of analysis provides some support for the importance of 'inside-out design', focusing on user needs rather than visual dominance.
Curvilinear effects for Complexity and Colour suggest intermediate levels are optimal for learning, balancing stimulation without over- or under-stimulation.
implementation_implications: Designers should consider a holistic approach using the SIN (Naturalness, Individualisation, Stimulation) model to address the complex interaction of environmental factors.
Prioritize naturalness factors (Light, Temperature, Air Quality) as they account for around 50% of the impact on learning.
Implement design strategies for optimal light: larger windows from orientations with no direct sun (glare), good shading control, high quality/quantity electrical lighting.
Ensure good thermal control: rooms with little sun heat, adequate external shading, radiators with thermostats for occupant control.
Improve air quality: large room volume, big window opening size at different heights, mechanical ventilation options.
Foster ownership: distinct design characteristics, personalized displays, high quality chairs/desks.
Provide flexibility: age-appropriate varied plan shapes, easy access to breakout/storage space, well-defined learning zones, large wall area for display.
Balance stimulation: room layout, ceiling, displays should be engaging but ordered, avoiding clutter. Use light/white walls with bright highlights/feature walls, bright colours as accents.

Recognize that some factors (e.g., Sound, Links to Nature, Connection) may show strong bivariate correlations but be competed out in multi-level models, suggesting their impact is integrated within other factors or less direct.
Focus on 'inside-out design' that builds from user needs rather than visual dominance, as school-level factors have muted impact compared to classroom-level factors.

limitations: The study focused on one type of building (primary schools) in one country (UK/England) and explains one measure of human performance (formal academic progress).
The pedagogy practiced in UK primary schools is distinctive, so the impact of the whole-building level could be more prominent in other scenarios.
Other factors or weighting of factors may be relevant to other dimensions of education, such as behavioral development.
Different requirements could pertain for different activities where the appropriate level of stimulation varies.
UK displays specific climatic conditions; optimum conditions would vary geographically, though basic human comfort needs are more stable.
Cultural differences could drive variations in pedagogy or preferences/reactions to colour.
Some currently judgmental measures (e.g., visual complexity) could be moved to objective measures in future research.
Teacher effects were assumed to be in the unexplained variance at the classroom level due to confidentiality concerns.
Data sensitivity and strict informed consent agreements prevent making underlying data available.
